findings: The scorer underestimates contra-risk when the right-hand fragment contains the single disambiguating, negating, or specifying element (negation, quantifier/ordinal, list continuation, or the complement that decides truth) that determines the truth-conditions of the already-heard left fragment.

The scorer treats coordinating/connective words (but, and, while, however, respectively, etc.) too lightly and therefore misses that cuts adjacent to these connectors typically indicate tight dependency or contrast and often carry high contra/cohesion risk.

findings: The prompt understates the risk when the right-hand fragment supplies the single obligatory element (a finite verb, nominal head, required complement, or explicit negation/reverser) that completes or sets the truth-conditions of the left; cutting there leaves the left fragment misleading or effectively contradicted when the right is heard alone.

The wording for the single-obligatory-element check was interpreted as encouraging isolation of the completing element on the right, and the noun-head/apposition guidance caused the model to avoid some noun-boundary cuts by shifting cuts into predicates and enumerations.
diagnosis.lesson: When revising, ensure checks discourage cutting between heads and their obligatory complements/appositions (don’t encourage isolating the completer on the right) because otherwise the model will shift cuts earlier and fragment predicates and enumerations, especially harming mid-length pieces.

findings: The prompt underestimates the risk of cutting a clause or predicate off from its single obligatory completer (subordinators, finite verbs, auxiliaries, quantifiers, or verbs that require a specific object), so it often scores cuts that isolate the completer on the right as acceptable even though the right fragment, when heard alone, changes or incompletes the earlier claim.

The prompt fails to penalize cuts that split a noun head from identifying modifiers or appositives (titles, names, restrictive modifiers), producing fragments that lose referential clarity or are misleading when heard alone.

diagnosis.why: Replacing C8 introduced explicit checks that penalize isolating tiny right‑hand completions and that try to catch noun‑head/apposition separations; this slightly helped very short piece decisions (≤3 words) but shifted top scoring cuts in mid/long bins so the model often cut earlier inside clauses (splitting verbs from adverbs and detaching appositives), lowering H_set overall.
diagnosis.lesson: When adding semantic checks, avoid asymmetric penalties that protect tiny right fragments at the cost of creating incentives to split heads from their modifiers or appositives—apply the checks so they do not encourage earlier, intra‑clausal cuts.

findings: The scorer underestimates contra risk when the right-hand fragment, however short, contains the clause-final predicate or any polarity/modality/corrective element that finalizes truth‑conditions; a tiny RHS that completes or flips the verb phrase can by itself overturn the meaning the listener has already heard and must be treated as high contra.

The scorer underestimates cohesion loss when a cut separates a head from its required complements or modifiers (noun heads and their post‑modifiers, subordinate openers and their complements, appositives): the left fragment may look self‑contained but leaves essential relations unresolved and yields poor joined meaning.

diagnosis.why: The two inserted checks made the scorer prefer attaching decisive predicates/complements to the left and penalize cuts that would leave 1–2 word completers on the right; that pushed many boundaries in very short pieces (≤3 and ≤5 words), producing isolated function words or single‑word fragments (e.g. isolated "by", "differently") and so hurt short‑bin H_set while modestly improving cohesion for longer fragments (bins ≥7).
diagnosis.lesson: Future edits should preserve natural short-piece attachments and avoid aggressive regrouping that creates isolated one‑word function/complement fragments, since the new contra/cohesion checks help longer spans but damage very short bins.
